catalog_quote: Syllables are (C)V(V)(C). ... All roots (including those of pronouns and particles) have underlying stress. Monosyllabic words retain stress only if they are of the ‟superheavy” form CVVC and/or precede pause; monosyllabic prefixes §6.1.2 are also unstressed. Bound and free words do not differ in stress behaviour; the term ‟clitic” will be reserved for left-bound words which partly or completely inhibit apocope of the preceding word §3.1. Prosodic enclitics §4.3 shift the stress of a preceding word to its last syllable. With the syllable as tone-bearing unit, there are four tones (strictly, tonemes): high (H), mid (M), low (L) and circumflex (X), as in gɛ́l ‛egg’, dūm ‛knee’, bʋ̀ŋ ‛donkey’, nû'ug ‛hand.’ ... Every syllable bears a tone, unless it has a reduced vowel §2.2. ... MH 🡒 MMꜜ before a stressed syllable, except at the end of questions; there is no downstep when the following ton…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Eddyshaw 2026 PDF/txt at sec. 2.3 pp. 26-28, and the supporting prefix statement at sec. 6.1.2 p. 127; the p. 28 example explicitly places stress on the post-prefix root syllable, matching our 'morphological (root/stem-initial) stress' coding. (2) Deciding source is a current 423-pp reference grammar with an explicit stress section — the top Glottolog grammar for the language and the only work found that analyses Kusaal stress; no JIPA illustration, instrumental study or stress article exists in Crossref. (3) What we lack are the native-speaker descriptions (Musah 2018 grammar, Musah 2010 MPhil, Musah 2017 weight chapter) and Niggli 2012 for Toende; none is open-access from here. Two open items fetched sources: Duah's 2020 review of Musah 2018 is silent on stress (tone-only phonology), and Abubakari & Appah 2024 p. 10 assert in one

sources.citation: Abubakari, Hasiyatu & Clement Kwamina Insaidoo Appah. 2024. Distinguishing compounds from phrases in Kusaal. Ghana Journal of Linguistics 13(2): 1-26. doi:10.4314/gjl.v13i2.1
sources.quote: 'Stress marking is generally not a characteristic of Kusaal and Mabia languages. For instance, Hudu (2010:19) asserts that "Dagbani and other Gur languages are not stress marking". Thus, this criterion cannot be applied to distinguish compounds from phrases in Kusaal.' — a one-sentence assertion (no data or analysis) by a native-speaker linguist that Kusaal has no stress; contradicts the existence of word stress rather than its location.

sources.citation: Duah, Reginald Akuoko. 2020. Editorial book critique: A Grammar of Kusaal: A Mabia language of Northern Ghana [review of Musah 2018]. Ghana Journal of Linguistics 9(2): 88-98. doi:10.4314/gjl.v9i2.5
sources.quote: Summarises Musah's ch. 2: 23 consonants, 9 vowels, ATR and rounding harmony, 'three register tones (high, mid, low)', TBU is 'the mora rather than the syllable'; no mention of stress anywhere in the review.

sources.citation: Musah, Anthony Agoswin. 2018. A Grammar of Kusaal: A Mabia (Gur) Language of Northern Ghana. (Schriften zur Afrikanistik.) Frankfurt am Main: Peter Lang. 281 pp. doi:10.3726/b14344
